title: Floating and Sinking
kicker: Cambridge Primary Checkpoint · Science 0097 · Stage 6 · Physics
summary: Understand why objects float or sink using weight and upthrust, and how changing the mass or the shape of an object can make it float or sink.

blocks.title: In the curriculum
items: Recognise that the **mass** of an object and its **shape** can both affect whether it **floats** or **sinks** (6Pf.05).

blocks.text: 1. Floating and sinking

An object **floats** when it stays at the surface of the water (part of it may be under the water). An object **sinks** when it goes down to the bottom. Whether something floats depends on two forces and on two properties of the object: its **mass** and its **shape**.

items: float
يطفو — stays at the surface of the water
sink
يغرق / يغوص — goes down to the bottom
upthrust
قوة الدفع لأعلى — the upward push of the water on an object
weight
الوزن — the downward pull of gravity, in newtons (N)
mass
الكتلة — the amount of matter in an object, in grams (g) or kilograms (kg)
shape
الشكل — the form of the object (ball, flat sheet, hollow boat…)
hollow
مجوّف — empty inside, usually full of air
cargo / load
الحمولة — the things a boat carries
plasticine / modelling clay
الصلصال — a soft material that can be moulded into any shape
aluminium foil
ورق الألومنيوم — thin metal sheet used to make model boats

blocks.text: 2. Two forces decide: weight and upthrust

Every object in water has two forces acting on it. **Weight** pulls it **down**. **Upthrust** from the water pushes it **up**. When you put an object in water, it pushes some water out of the way. The **more water it pushes aside, the bigger the upthrust**.

items: **Floats:** the object sinks into the water only until the upthrust has grown to equal its weight. Upthrust = weight, the forces are **balanced**, and it stays at the surface.
**Sinks:** even when the whole object is under the water, the upthrust is still smaller than the weight. Weight > upthrust, the forces are **unbalanced** and the overall force is downwards.

blocks.text: **You can measure upthrust with a forcemeter.** Hang a stone from a forcemeter: in air it reads its weight, for example 6 N. Lower the stone into water and the reading drops, for example to 4 N. The water is pushing up with **6 − 4 = 2 N** of upthrust. (The stone's mass has not changed — the water is just helping to hold it up.) You can also feel upthrust when you try to push a beach ball under the water.
3. How shape affects floating

Take a 50 g lump of plasticine. Roll it into a ball and drop it into water: it **sinks**. Now press the **same** plasticine into a wide, thin, hollow boat shape: it **floats**. The mass is the same, so the weight is the same — only the shape has changed.

blocks.caption: The same mass of plasticine. As a ball it sinks; as a wide, hollow boat it floats.

blocks.text: **Why?** The wide, hollow shape is full of air and spreads over a large area, so it pushes aside a lot more water before it is under the surface. More water pushed aside means **more upthrust**, enough to balance the weight. The small ball can only push aside a little water, so its upthrust stays smaller than its weight.

This is why huge ships made of steel float. A solid block of steel would sink, but a ship is a hollow shape full of air. The steel is spread out into a wide hull that pushes aside a very large amount of water.
4. How mass affects floating

Now keep the **shape** the same and change the **mass**. Put cargo into a floating boat: the boat sits **lower** in the water, because more of it must be under water to push aside enough water to balance the bigger weight. Keep adding cargo and at last the boat cannot push aside enough water — water comes over the sides and the boat **sinks**.

blocks.text: Another example: two identical plastic bottles with their lids on. The empty bottle floats high. The same bottle filled with sand has much more mass, so it sinks. Same shape and size, different mass, different result.

rows: Make the object a wider, hollow shape
More water pushed aside → more upthrust → more likely to **float**
Squash the object into a small ball
Less water pushed aside → less upthrust → more likely to **sink**

blocks.title: "Heavy things sink" is NOT the rule
blocks.text: A ship of thousands of tonnes floats, but a small coin or a paper clip sinks. You must think about **both** the mass and the shape. A good Checkpoint answer names the property (mass or shape) **and** links it to the forces (upthrust and weight).

blocks.title: بالعربي — افتكر القاعدة دي
items: على أي جسم في المية قوتين: الوزن (weight) لتحت، وقوة الدفع (upthrust) لفوق.
يطفو (float) لما الدفع = الوزن. يغرق (sink) لما الوزن أكبر من الدفع.
الشكل (shape): نفس الصلصال لو عملته كورة يغرق، ولو عملته مركب عريض مجوف يطفو، لأنه بيزق مية أكتر فالدفع يكبر.
الكتلة (mass): كل ما تحط حمولة أكتر في المركب ينزل في المية أكتر، ولو زودت قوي يغرق.
مش كل حاجة تقيلة بتغرق — السفينة الحديد بتطفو بسبب شكلها.

blocks.text: 5. Investigating shape: the foil boat challenge

Nadia wants to find out **how the size of the base of a foil boat affects how many marbles it can hold before it sinks**. She cuts four squares of foil, all 20 cm × 20 cm, and folds each into a boat with a square base of a different size. She adds marbles one at a time and counts how many the boat holds before it sinks. She repeats each test three times.

rows: the size of the base of the boat (its shape)
the number of marbles the boat holds before it sinks
size and type of foil (so every boat has the same mass); same size and type of marbles; same container of water; marbles added gently to the middle of the boat

blocks.text: **Conclusion:** the wider the base of the boat, the more marbles it holds before it sinks, because a wider boat pushes aside more water and so gets more upthrust. The increase gets smaller for the widest boats, because their sides become very low and water comes over the top sooner. This shows that **shape** affects floating. Adding marbles shows the effect of **mass**: every boat sinks once the mass of marbles is too big.
6. Worked examples
**Worked example 1** — A block floats in water. Its weight is 4 N. (a) What is the size of the upthrust on the block? [1] (b) Explain your answer. [1]

**Answer:** (a) **4 N**. (b) The block is floating (not moving up or down), so the forces are **balanced**: upthrust = weight. **Common mistake:** thinking upthrust must be bigger than weight for something to float. If upthrust were bigger, the object would rise until it balanced.
**Worked example 2** — A stone hangs from a forcemeter. The reading is 8 N in air and 5 N when the stone is under water. Work out the upthrust. Show your working. [2]

blocks.text: **Working:** upthrust = reading in air − reading in water = 8 − 5 = **3 N**. **Common mistake:** writing 5 N (the reading in water) — that is not the upthrust; it is what the forcemeter still has to hold.

**Worked example 3** — Ali makes a ball and a boat from two equal pieces of plasticine. The ball sinks and the boat floats. (a) Which variable is the same for the two objects? [1] (b) Explain why the boat floats. [2]

items: (a) **mass** (so also the weight; also accept: the material).

(b) The boat shape is wide/hollow so it **pushes aside more water** (1 mark), so the **upthrust is bigger and equals the weight** (1 mark). The ball pushes aside less water, so upthrust < weight and it sinks.

blocks.text: **Worked example 4** — A toy boat floats in a bath. Sara puts coins into it one by one. Describe and explain what happens. [2]

**Answer:** The boat floats **lower and lower** in the water as the coins are added, because its mass (weight) increases (1 mark). When there are too many coins, the upthrust cannot balance the weight / water comes over the side, so the boat **sinks** (1 mark).
**Worked example 5** — Look at Nadia's results table above. (a) Which result for the 10 cm base would be anomalous if Test 3 had been 12 marbles? [1] (b) What should Nadia do with it? [1]

**Answer:** (a) **12**, because it is far lower than the other results (25 and 26) for the same boat. (b) **Repeat** that test (or leave it out when working out the mean) — and check what went wrong, e.g. the foil was torn or marbles were dropped in roughly.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
items: Writing "heavy objects sink and light objects float". Shape matters too — a heavy steel ship floats.
Saying a floating object has **no** weight, or that upthrust is **bigger** than weight. For a floating object they are **equal**.
Saying the mass of the plasticine changed when the shape changed. Same plasticine = same mass.
Explaining only "because of its shape" — you must add **why**: it pushes aside more water, so there is more upthrust.
In investigations, forgetting to keep the mass of foil the same when testing shape (it would not be a fair test).

blocks.title: How Checkpoint asks this
items: **Predict** whether an object floats or sinks after its shape or mass changes, then **explain** using upthrust and weight.
**Add arrows** for upthrust and weight to a diagram of a floating object — same length for floating, longer weight arrow for sinking.
**Plasticine / foil boat investigations:** name the independent, dependent and control variables, spot the anomalous result, say why tests are repeated, describe the pattern in a table or bar chart.
**Forcemeter readings** in air and in water: subtract to find the upthrust, and read the scale carefully.
Two-mark explain questions usually need: the property (mass/shape) **+** the forces (more water pushed aside → more upthrust; or more mass → more weight).

blocks.intro: Use the words weight, upthrust, mass and shape in your explanations. Check each worked solution after you answer.

questions.q: A plastic duck floats on water. Which statement about the forces on it is correct?
c: The weight is bigger than the upthrust.
The upthrust is equal to the weight.
questions.e: A floating object is not moving up or down, so the forces are balanced: upthrust = weight.

questions.q: Name the upward force that water puts on an object in it.
questions.e: Upthrust is the upward push of the water.

questions.q: A metal key weighs 0.6 N in air. When it hangs under water from a forcemeter, the reading is 0.4 N. Work out the upthrust on the key.
Rana has four pieces of plasticine with the same mass. Which shape is most likely to float?
questions.e: A wide, hollow dish pushes aside the most water, so it gets the biggest upthrust — enough to balance its weight.

questions.q: A large ship is made of steel, but it floats. Why?
c: Its hollow shape pushes aside a lot of water, so the upthrust is big.
The engines push the ship up.
questions.e: The ship is a wide hollow shape full of air; it pushes aside a very large amount of water, giving enough upthrust to balance its weight.

questions.q: More bags are loaded onto a floating boat. What happens to the boat?
c: It floats higher in the water.
It floats lower in the water.
questions.e: More mass means more weight, so the boat sinks deeper until the extra water it pushes aside gives enough upthrust to balance it.

questions.q: Two identical plastic bottles have their lids on. Bottle A is empty. Bottle B is full of sand. One floats and one sinks. Which bottle sinks: A or B?
questions.e: Bottle B has much more mass (and weight) but the same shape, so its weight is bigger than the upthrust and it sinks.

questions.q: A wooden block floats. The upthrust on it is 2.5 N. What is the weight of the block?
questions.e: Floating means balanced forces: weight = upthrust = 2.5 N.

questions.p: Yusuf folds four squares of foil, all the same size, into boats with different shapes. He counts how many marbles each boat holds before it sinks.
questions.q: (a) What is the independent variable in Yusuf's investigation?
c: the size of the foil squares
questions.e: The independent variable is what he changes on purpose: the shape of the boat.

questions.p: Yusuf folds four squares of foil, all the same size, into boats with different shapes. He counts how many marbles each boat holds before it sinks.
questions.q: (b) For one boat he gets these results: 22 marbles, 21 marbles, 9 marbles. Which number is the anomalous result?
questions.e: 9 does not fit the pattern of the other two results (about 21–22), so it is anomalous. He should repeat that test.

questions.p: Yusuf folds four squares of foil, all the same size, into boats with different shapes. He counts how many marbles each boat holds before it sinks.
questions.q: (c) Explain why Yusuf used foil squares that were all the same size. [1]
questions.ms: 1 mark: so the boats all have the same mass / so only the shape changes / to make it a fair test. Do not accept 'to make it easier'.
questions.e: Same-sized foil squares have the same mass, so mass is controlled and only the shape changes — a fair test.

questions.q: A 30 g ball of plasticine sinks in water. Explain how Leila could make the **same** plasticine float, and why this works. [2]
questions.ms: 1 mark: change its shape into a boat / wide, flat, hollow dish (with sides). 1 mark: it pushes aside more water, so the upthrust increases (to equal the weight). Do not accept 'make it lighter' (the plasticine must stay the same).
questions.e: Mould it into a wide, hollow boat shape with sides. It then pushes aside more water, so the upthrust gets bigger and can balance its weight, so it floats.

c: Both mass and shape can affect whether an object floats.
questions.e: Mass and shape both matter: heavy ships float because of their shape, and small light coins can sink.

questions.q: A floating foil boat holds 15 marbles. Mona adds marbles one at a time. Describe what happens to the boat as marbles are added, and explain why it finally sinks. [2]
questions.ms: 1 mark: the boat floats lower / sits deeper in the water as each marble is added. 1 mark: the mass/weight becomes bigger than the upthrust (the water can no longer hold it up / water comes over the sides), so it sinks.
questions.e: Each marble adds mass, so the boat sits lower to push aside more water. Once the weight is more than the biggest upthrust the boat can get (water comes over the sides), it sinks.

blocks.title: Remember
items: Weight acts down; **upthrust** from the water acts up.
Floats: upthrust = weight. Sinks: weight > upthrust.
**Shape:** a wide, hollow shape pushes aside more water → more upthrust → more likely to float.
**Mass:** more mass → floats lower → too much mass and it sinks.
Upthrust from a forcemeter = reading in air − reading in water.
Heavy things do not always sink — always think about mass AND shape.
